sections.title: Clinical Definition & Hemodynamics
sections.content: Carotid-cavernous fistulae (CCF) represent an arteriovenous shunt where blood flows directly or indirectly from the internal or external carotid arteries into the cavernous sinus. This reverses the normal pressure gradient, leading to venous hypertension in the ophthalmic veins, causing 'arterialization' of the conjunctival vessels and orbital congestion.

rows: Mild features, often spontaneous in post-menopausal women.
Slow onset, localized to orbital congestion.
Meningeal branches of both ICA and ECA
Most common 'indirect' type; can mimic chronic conjunctivitis.

sections.title: The Dandy's Triad of Direct CCF
EMERGENCY: Vision-Threatening Red Flags
content: Rapidly declining Visual Acuity (Compressive Optic Neuropathy)
IOP > 40 mmHg (Secondary Glaucoma risk)
Pulsatile Exophthalmos with Cornea Exposure
Severe Intracranial Hemorrhage signs
Abrupt worsening of Proptosis (Venous Thrombosis risk)

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Corkscrew epibulbar vessels: Dilated, tortuous vessels reaching the limbus.
Ophthalmoplegia: CN VI is most common (intracavernous), followed by III and IV.
Raised IOP: Due to increased episcleral venous pressure and choroidal effusions.
Fundus: Dilated retinal veins, intraretinal hemorrhages, disc edema (Venous Stasis Retinopathy).
RAPD: Positive if there is significant optic nerve compression or ischemic neuropathy.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Sequence
content: 1. Bedside Auscultation: Listen for bruit over the globe or temple.
2. Non-Invasive Imaging: CTA or MRA to look for 'flow voids' and SOV enlargement.
3. B-Scan Ultrasound: Identify dilated Superior Ophthalmic Vein (SOV).
4. Formal Gold Standard: Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA) for definitive mapping.
5. Tonometry/Gonioscopy: Assess IOP and angle neovascularization.

rows: Confirms the exact site of the fistula.

content.explanation: A: Artery (ICA direct), B: Branches of ICA, C: Carotid (External) branches, D: Dual (Both ICA/ECA branches).

sections.title: Management Hierarchy
content: Step 1: Observation - Indicated for low-flow (Type B,C,D) as 50-70% may spontaneously thrombose.
Step 2: Carotid Massage - Digital compression of the carotid artery to induce thrombosis (only for low-flow).
Step 3: Endovascular Intervention - First-line for Direct CCF. Transarterial or transvenous coiling.
Step 4: Embolic Agents - Use of detachable coils, Onyx, or N-butyl cyanoacrylate (NBCA).
Step 5: Surgical Ligation - Historically significant, but rarely used in the modern endovascular era.

sections.title: Surgical & Endovascular Techniques
content: Transvenous route: Often accessed via the Inferior Petrosal Sinus.
SOV Cutdown: Surgical exposure of the Superior Ophthalmic Vein for coil delivery if other routes fail.
Flow-Diverting Stents: Emerging technology for complex ICA wall defects.
Balloon Occlusion: Detachable balloons (though less common now than coils).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: The 'White-Eyed CCF': Indirect fistulae can present very subtly, mimicking chronic conjunctivitis that doesn't respond to drops.
Trauma + Bruit: Post-head injury patient with a pulse-synchronous sound is Type A until proven otherwise.
Paradoxical Worsening: Symptoms may worsen immediately after successful treatment due to temporary thrombosis-related inflammation.
The 6th Nerve: CN VI is the most vulnerable as it sits freely within the cavernous sinus.

rows: Cortical venous reflux from the shunt.

sections.title: Landmark Study: Barrow et al. (1985)
sections.content: The seminal paper 'Vascular malformations of the cavernous sinus' established the A-D classification system. It remains the clinical foundation for determining whether a fistula requires urgent endovascular intervention (High-flow Type A) or can be managed conservatively (Low-flow Types B-D).

sections.content: A Carotid-Cavernous Fistula is an abnormal communication between the carotid arterial system and the cavernous sinus. It represents a complex neuro-ophthalmic emergency that requires precise classification and multi-disciplinary management to prevent permanent vision loss or intracranial catastrophe.

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: A Carotid-Cavernous Fistula (CCF) is a high- or low-flow communication between the internal or external carotid arteries (or their branches) and the cavernous sinus. This results in high-pressure arterial blood entering the low-pressure venous cavernous sinus, leading to venous engorgement of the orbit and globe. It is a potentially sight-threatening and life-threatening condition depending on the flow dynamics and venous drainage patterns.

rows: Direct shunt between ICA and Cavernous Sinus
Dural shunt: Meningeal branches of ICA
Dural shunt: Meningeal branches of ECA
Dural shunt: Meningeal branches of ICA + ECA

content.explanation: P: Pulsatile Proptosis (with thrill). C: Conjunctival Chemosis (corkscrew vessels). B: Bruit (heard over the globe or temple).

sections.title: Red Flags: Impending Danger
content: Cortical Venous Reflux (High risk of ICH/Stroke)
Rapidly Progressive Visual Loss (AION or Glaucoma)
Massive Epistaxis (Rupture into Sphenoid Sinus)
New-onset 3rd, 4th, or 6th Nerve Palsy

sections.title: Comprehensive Clinical Features
content: Corkscrew Vessels: Dilated, tortuous epibulbar veins reaching the limbus.
Increased Intraocular Pressure (IOP): Due to elevated episcleral venous pressure and choroidal effusions.
Ophthalmoplegia: Usually CN VI (intracavernous) first, followed by III and IV.
Pulsatile Proptosis: Best seen by observing the patient's profile or with an exophthalmometer.
Fundus Findings: Venous dilation, disc edema, intraretinal hemorrhages (Central Retinal Vein Occlusion-like).
Anterior Segment: Ischemia, corneal edema, iris neovascularization (rare).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Hierarchy
content: 1. Clinical Auscultation: Listening for a bruit with a stethoscope diaphragm over the globe.
2. Non-Invasive Imaging: CTA or MRA to identify enlarged Superior Ophthalmic Veins (SOV).
3. Ultrasound: B-scan/Color Doppler showing reversed (arterialized) flow in the SOV.
4. Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA): The GOLD STANDARD to identify the shunt site and venous drainage.
5. Tonometry: High-amplitude ocular pulsations on Goldmann Tonometry.

rows: Bilateral usually, EOM enlargement (tendon sparing), no bruit.
Fever, leukocytosis, pain on eye movement, no pulsation.
Acute onset pain, dramatic response to steroids.
Systemic illness, rapid progression, usually secondary to infection.

sections.title: Medical Management Protocol
content: IOP Control: Beta-blockers, Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors (avoid miotics).
Lubrication: Management of exposure keratopathy.
Observation: Appropriate for low-flow dural CCFs (Type B-D) as 50% may spontaneously close.
Carotid Massage: 10 mins/hour in selected low-flow cases (contraindicated in carotid stenosis).

content.explanation: O: Oculomotor (III), T: Trochlear (IV), O: Ophthalmic (V1), M: Maxillary (V2). C: Carotid (ICA), A: Abducens (VI), T: T (Structural mnemonic).

sections.title: Ocular Complications & Prognosis
content: Secondary Angle-Closure Glaucoma (Choroidal effusion).
Cystoid Macular Edema (CME).
Proliferative Retinopathy (Hypoxia induced).
Permanent Cranial Nerve Palsy.
Post-treatment transient increase in symptoms (Normal).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Exam High-Yields
content: Dural CCFs are often misdiagnosed as 'chronic conjunctivitis' due to the red eye.
If IOP is high and the eye is pulsing, think CCF first.
The 6th nerve is the most common palsy because it sits freely within the cavernous sinus next to the ICA.
Venous drainage to the contralateral cavernous sinus can cause 'bilateral' symptoms from a 'unilateral' fistula.
Superior Ophthalmic Vein (SOV) diameter > 2mm on CT is highly suggestive of CCF.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Evidence
sections.content: Recent studies emphasize the use of Onyx (ethylene vinyl alcohol copolymer) for more durable dural fistula closure compared to coils alone. The trans-inferior petrosal sinus (IPS) remains the preferred transvenous route; however, when the IPS is thrombosed, direct orbital access to the SOV via lid crease incision is a highly successful secondary technique used by combined neuro-interventional and ophthalmic plastic surgery teams.
